projects.title: Starship Booster Cryo Proof Tooling
projects.summary: I redesigned Super Heavy’s cryo-proof tooling to reduce leak paths and make installation repeatable. My work covered welded drain elbows, self-clocking blankoffs, a GOX seal interface, and assembly-level integration.

points.text: I reviewed the tooling sealing 33 engine feedlines for unnecessary leak joints and difficult installation steps. I replaced bolted interfaces with welded connections where practical, rerouted drain tubes for work access, and revised remaining bolted connections to use standard hardware.

The drain-to-blankoff interface had a bolted stackup with several potential leak paths. I replaced it with a 90° elbow welded to the blankoff, leaving one B-nut joint to the flared drain tube through an AN connection with a copper seal. I chose 304 stainless steel to match the blankoff’s weld material.

Outlet orientation had to repeat across different blankoffs. I added a radial key and mating cutout to clock the elbow, plus a diameter step to locate its height for welding. I toleranced the fit to keep the TIG weld root gap within the specified 0.5 mm maximum.

points.lead: Loads: size the weld and recheck the part
points.text: I sized the elbow weld using Blodgett’s method and the maximum outlet moment from tank-pressure blow-off loads. The clocking cutout changed the blankoff geometry enough to require new analysis, so I checked each revised blankoff in Ansys under internal pressure.

points.lead: GOX port: weld and seal geometry
points.text: I eliminated another bolted leak interface by designing a Monel bung welded to a stainless blankoff. I toleranced the interface to minimize gaseous-oxygen (GOX) impingement risk and sized the dissimilar-metal weld using Blodgett’s method. The bung formed the inner lip of the upper seal gland, which I sized for the required O-ring compression using the Parker O-Ring Handbook.

Empirical testing showed the Teflon O-ring was more consistent and reliable than the spring-energized alternative under evaluation. Elsewhere in the assembly, I redesigned a subtly asymmetric welded subassembly so it could not be installed incorrectly.

I evaluated manufacturing deviations against critical sealing requirements and oversaw welded-subassembly fabrication and vehicle integration. I maintained the 13,000-component CAD assembly across three vehicles at different release states, and designed lineside storage and material flow to support two vehicles using the tooling simultaneously.

projects.note: Design work performed at SpaceX is proprietary. No CAD, drawings, part numbers, or hardware imagery are shown.

projects.title: Starship Production Tooling
projects.summary: On SpaceX’s Structures Build Engineering team, I helped design and build a new weld-focused subassembly cell for a high-pressure propulsion manifold for Starship V3. My work included flange fit-up fixtures, lift and access tooling, flight-part retrofits, and production improvements.

points.text: I helped design the manifold subassembly cell and designed self-clocking endpoint-flange fixtures. I used locating features and GD&T to control flange position and orientation for welding, then oversaw the cell’s integration on the production floor.

points.lead: Lift tool: size and prove the load path
points.text: I designed a manifold lift tool for a 1,100 lb working load limit, using bending and weld calculations to size it. The tool was proof-tested at twice that limit, or 2,200 lb.

I designed an integration jig for Starship’s aft flap torque frames to improve technician access. I developed the assembly sequence and used integration loads in bending and torsion to size the base, plates, and welds.

I designed five flight-part retrofits to accommodate off-nominal conditions in existing assemblies. I took precise measurements of the as-built hardware, created CAD models of those assemblies, and used them to define custom parts for manufacture and installation.
I also designed 3D-printed parts and parts manufactured through Protolabs to improve the build process.

projects.proof: GD&T-controlled flange fixtures, a 2,200 lb lift proof test, and five flight-part retrofits.
projects.takeaway: Locate the hardware accurately, then design around how it will be assembled.

projects.title: Brake Rotors & Mounts
projects.summary: I designed the rotor and mount for reliable braking within the drivetrain package, combining material tradeoffs, thermal analysis, structural FEA, and temperature testing.

points.text: I compared cast iron and 4140 steel and selected steel for its endurance-limit advantage. Titanium buttons limited heat transfer into the 7075 aluminum mount, which I packaged at the differential bolts.

points.lead: Thickness: bound and refine the heat load
points.text: For the 500°C requirement, I first sized thickness assuming maximum braking energy became heat with no heat escaping. I refined that conservative estimate with transient conduction, forced convection, and radiation analysis.

points.lead: Geometry: manage debris and check stress
points.text: I added curved face slots for debris removal, de-gassing, and water clearance, accepting additional pad wear. In Ansys, I supported the pad contact regions and applied braking moment through the mount connections to check stress.
I used temperature crayons to assess rotor operating temperatures and prepared the design for three-axis CNC manufacturing.

projects.headline: Brake Rotors & Mounts
projects.challenge: Coordinate the rotor packaging with the powertrain team and design for long-term reliability, with a 500°C temperature requirement and a safety margin.
projects.decision: Compare cast iron with 4140 steel, use titanium buttons to limit heat flow into an aluminum mount, and refine rotor thickness through transient thermal analysis.
projects.proof: Checked the rotor in Ansys with supports at the pad contact regions and braking moment applied through the mount bolt locations. Used temperature crayons to assess operating temperatures and outsourced manufacturing to a three-axis CNC supplier.
projects.takeaway: Long-term reliability guided the material choices, thermal sizing, and structural checks.

caliperSelection.rationale: Sponsorship availability was the deciding factor. The Brembo had the largest listed pad area, tied the ISR for the largest listed piston area, and weighed less than the ISR. The AP Racing option was lighter and the Wilwood was less expensive; the comparison did not identify a clear winner across all criteria.

projects.title: Rear Wheel Hub & Bearing Assembly
projects.summary: I designed a rear hub and bearing assembly that brought the drivetrain, wheel, and electronics interfaces together in a lightweight, manufacturable package.

points.text: I defined the hub around the drivetrain’s tripod bearing and the electronics team’s Hall sensors. I screened bearings in SKF SimPro Quick for load capacity, fatigue life, and power loss within an 80–85 mm bore and 110–120 mm outer-diameter envelope; the selection set hub thickness and packaging.
I compared titanium, 6061, and 7075 aluminum and selected 7075-T6. Its higher yield strength than 6061 supported the hub’s structural requirements.

I applied wheel loads from the team’s truss solver to the wheel flange, modeled the tensile load from the center-lock nut, and included bearing forces and drivetrain torque at the tripod interface. I sized hub-nut engagement using bolt tensile and nut thread-shear areas.

I built the geometry around the interfaces and selected bearing, removed excess material through pocketing, and checked the revised hub in Ansys. Rotational features were turned first; CNC milling produced the tripod cutout, pin and button holes, and flange pockets.

projects.headline: Rear Wheel Hub & Bearing Assembly
projects.challenge: Define a rear hub assembly around the drivetrain’s tripod bearing and the electronics team’s Hall effect sensors, while meeting structural and manufacturing requirements.
projects.decision: Use the system interfaces and bearing selection to establish the hub geometry and thickness, compare titanium with 6061 and 7075 aluminum, then size the threaded hub nut connection and optimize pocketing with FEA.
projects.proof: Checked cornering and braking loads, bearing performance in SKF SimPro Quick, and hub behavior in Ansys. Manufacturing included lathe operations on several features and tooling the part for a three-axis CNC mill.
projects.takeaway: The drivetrain and electronics interfaces set the requirements. Bearing selection, structural analysis, and machining constraints then shaped the hub.

bearingSelection.method: Build the assembly in SKF SimPro Quick and sweep the candidate bearings. Work with Powertrain to set the allowable inner diameter.
bearingSelection.validation: Selected the SKF 71817 ACDGB/VQ253 angular-contact bearing after reviewing fatigue life, load capacity, and power loss across wheel speeds.

projects.title: Carbon Pushrod & Swept Control Arms
projects.summary: I developed and fabricated a lighter suspension assembly, pairing carbon-fiber pushrods with steel control arms and checking both the bonded joints and on-car clearance.

points.lead: Materials: reduce mass within shop capability
points.text: I kept steel control arms because the team had greater confidence in that manufacturing process, and switched the pushrods to carbon fiber to reduce mass. Apex-mounted gussets replaced a heavy mounting plate.

I tested the carbon-fiber pushrods in tension and compression on an Instron. For fabrication, I cut the tubes to length and turned aluminum end plugs, controlling the bonding-surface diameter to within half a thousandth of an inch.

points.lead: Fabrication: carry the geometry into hardware
points.text: I cut steel tubing, turned and milled end plugs, bored and reamed bearing seats in laser-cut plates, and welded and tapped the plugs for rod ends.

During freshman-year integration, a missed tolerance stackup caused the apex to interfere at maximum steer. We checked the required material removal in Ansys and ground the existing apex to recover clearance. The combined suspension redesign saved 4.6 lb.

projects.headline: Pushrods & Control Arms
projects.unit: less suspension mass than the prior design
projects.challenge: At integration, the control-arm apex interfered before the car reached maximum steer. A tolerance stackup we had missed in the design caused the clearance problem.
projects.decision: Model the exact material removal needed at the apex, check the revised geometry in Ansys, then use an angle grinder to remove that material from the existing part.
projects.proof: The revised apex made maximum steer possible. The original suspension redesign saved 4.6 lb through the apex-mounted gussets and carbon-fiber pushrods.
projects.takeaway: That experience taught me how much engineering is working through the problem in front of you, one constraint at a time.

projects.title: Discrete Ride Height Adjustment
projects.summary: I designed a shim-based attachment to make ride-height changes more repeatable, replacing a process that relied on turning an opposite-thread pushrod.

points.text: The mechanism changes pushrod length by adding or removing shims and retightening the fasteners. The attachment connects to the inboard suspension mechanism and keeps the shim stack in compression.
I designed the attachment in 7075 aluminum and kept the shim pockets concentric with the retaining bolts. Lightweight shim geometry reduced the mass added by the adjustment mechanism.

I checked the attachment under pushrod loading in SolidWorks FEA. The shims were laser-cut and the attachment pieces machined; another team member CNC-machined the upper component. The mechanism added 0.7 lb across the car in exchange for repeatable adjustment.

projects.unit: added to the entire car for adjustability
projects.challenge: Make trackside ride-height changes more repeatable and easier to perform.
projects.decision: Use a 7075 aluminum attachment with removable shims for repeatable ride-height adjustment.
projects.proof: SolidWorks FEA checked the attachment under pushrod loading. The mechanism added 0.7 lb across the car.
projects.takeaway: A small weight penalty bought a more repeatable adjustment for the team at the track.
